options.text: There is an opportunity because President-elect Trump said during the campaign that there was a real opportunity for the United States to support Russia and the Assad regime in their battle against ISIS, and I presume the president-elect probably understands that there is no Russian-Assad regime battle against ISIS, and that the tactics being used by Russia and Assad against civilian populations are in fact a wonderful recruiting tool and a gift that keeps on giving for ISIS.

There is no chance for a strategic reset because the humanitarian catastrophe engineered by the regime in Damascus and Russian warplanes targeting hospitals in East Aleppo has ruined any diplomatic leverage. United Nations envoy Staffan de Mistura and European Union leaders in Brussels recognize that Bashar al-Assad is a war criminal who must face the International Criminal Court in The Hague. The incoming White House team under Donald Trump cannot legitimize Vladimir Putin’s brutal military campaign.
options.why: Answer 1 affirms that there is an opportunity to change course in Syria, whereas Answer 2 explicitly states that there is no chance for such a change.

options.text: The incoming Washington administration should increase support for moderate Syrian opposition units under the High Negotiations Committee banner, funded by Saudi Arabia and Qatar. President Barack Obama made a serious mistake by not enforcing his red lines against Bashar al-Assad's chemical weapons use near Damascus. If Donald Trump abandons the Free Syrian Army, fighters trained by the CIA in Jordan and Turkey will disappear, handing a permanent victory to Tehran and Moscow.
options.why: Answer 1 suggests cooperating with Russia and Assad against ISIS, whereas Answer 2 argues for increasing support for the moderate opposition to counter Russia, Assad, and Iran.

options.text: No, because Syrian military forces under President Bashar al-Assad, alongside our Iranian allies and General Qasem Soleimani’s Revolutionary Guard, are fighting extremist factions like Jabhat Fateh al-Sham. Washington politicians like Senator John McCain and Secretary John Kerry misread the ground reality in Aleppo and Damascus. President-elect Donald Trump must understand that working with Vladimir Putin’s Kremlin is the only viable path to stabilize the Levant and destroy terror networks.
options.why: Answer 1 affirms that there is an opportunity to change course by recognizing the destructive nature of Russia and Assad's tactics, whereas Answer 2 argues there is no opportunity to change course because the current alliance fighting extremists (including Assad and Russia) is already the correct path.

options.text: Not anymore, since those independent militias have lost all their credibility and territorial control. Back during the early battles in Idlib and Daraa, groups like Ahrar al-Sham offered a democratic alternative to Bashar al-Assad. However, rampant corruption and internal factionalism ruined them. Any foreign assistance from the Pentagon or NATO would be utterly wasted on a fragmented movement that cannot govern its own captured towns or protect local citizens.
options.why: Answer 1 affirms that a viable nationalist movement still exists to be supported, whereas Answer 2 explicitly denies this, stating that such groups have lost all credibility and control.

options.text: That movement is entirely gone, so foreign governments have nobody reliable left to support. Years ago, moderate councils in places like Homs and Deir ez-Zor showed real promise against the regime in Damascus. Yet relentless Russian airstrikes and Iranian ground offensives decimated those leaders. Right now, supplying arms through Turkey or Jordan only prolongs a stalemate without empowering any coherent political alternative capable of ruling a post-war nation.
options.why: Answer 1 affirms that a viable nationalist movement still exists to be supported, whereas Answer 2 asserts that this movement is entirely gone and leaves no reliable partner for foreign backing.

options.text: Yes, I believe there is. But I think our support should focus on civilian protection. For the people of Syria and the West, this has had political consequences too. For example, there is a direct line between the huge migrant crisis that affected Europe mostly in 2015, driven largely by Syria, and the vote in the United Kingdom to leave the European Union.

No, because that faction has completely disintegrated on the ground there. Back when the Free Syrian Army held territory near Damascus and Aleppo, intervention might have mattered. But today, extremist groups like Jabhat Fateh al-Sham and ISIS completely dominate the opposition forces. If Washington or London sends money or weaponry now, it simply ends up in the hands of jihadists fighting against Western interests across the Middle East.
options.why: Answer 1 affirms that a nationalist movement still exists to be supported, whereas Answer 2 denies this, arguing that the faction has completely disintegrated.

options.text: Many fighters leaving Homs and Hama share the exact same radical ideology as Daesh, and once they regroup in the eastern desert near Raqqa, commanders like Zahran Alloush will likely merge their brigades directly into the Islamic State.

options.text: Anyone who considers himself a Syrian nationalist, meaning a Syria-firster, would find it very difficult to join ISIS because ISIS believes it has a worldwide mission, and ISIS has not been fighting Bashar al-Assad very much anyway.
